title: Met with the Mayor and CEO of the City of Nedlands
body: Community representatives met with Mayor Leonie Browner, CEO Paul Martin and City of Nedlands planning staff on 14 September 2026 to brief them on the project in detail. The City raised its own concerns about how the proposal sits against the Mount Claremont Masterplan, noted it had previously asked the State for a briefing without response, and confirmed it will follow up again directly with the responsible department. Full detail, and our follow-up letter to the City, on the Correspondence page.
linkText: Read the full update on the Correspondence page

title: Reply received from the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist
body: A reply arrived from the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist, 28 days after our letter. It doesn't directly address any of the nine questions we asked — though we think two of them arguably weren't its place to answer before the facility comes to it for formal authorisation. Its own newly-published standard for infrastructure projects raises a more specific, still-open question than the one it did answer. Full comparison, including what we think is and isn't fair to expect, is on the Correspondence page.
linkText: Read the full comparison on the Correspondence page

title: New: Infrastructure WA's own numbers on the buffer fix — not approved, and not until the 2030s
body: Infrastructure WA has published its assessment of Water Corporation's plan for a new $1.3 billion treatment plant at the same site as the buffer we've already written about — closely related to, though not confirmed as identical to, the Market Led Proposal referenced on that page. Its own figures show planning starting in 2026–27 and commissioning "complete in the early 2030s" at best — and reducing the odour buffer itself is treated as a separate, unapproved step, needing its own government go-ahead just to begin investigating. The assessment is dated December 2025; it wasn't made public for a further six months, alongside media confirmation that the $1.3 billion project as a whole still isn't approved. It doesn't tell us what Graylands' own planning assumes about the buffer — that's still the open question behind FOI Request 9 — but it does rule out one answer: whatever the Minister meant by "considered" in July 2025, it wasn't a funded, dated fix, because none exists.
linkText: Read the updated odour buffer page

title: This already happened once — the full 1990 parliamentary record
body: WA Parliament Hansard for 8 May and 29 November 1990 shows this exact plan was warned about, in detail, 36 years ago: a 646-signature petition asking for consultation before any decision, and a Legislative Assembly speech naming the same failures now on the public record — two written assurances to this neighbourhood already broken, absconding patients already causing off-site harm, and a prediction that moving offenders through security levels without a buffer zone made further harm inevitable. The MP who gave that speech, Colin Barnett, went on to serve as Premier of Western Australia from 2008 to 2017 — and was Premier in October 2014 when the exact failure he'd warned about happened on his own watch. Full transcripts and a complete account are now published.

title: First look at what's actually being built: 3.54 hectares of new secure ground
body: The government's own environmental consultant states it directly: the two new secure compounds Stage 1 adds will disturb 3.54 hectares between them — buildings, courtyards, secure perimeters and buffer zones combined, close to five football pitches. That's the Adult Secure Main Entry cluster on John XXIII Avenue and a separate Child and Adolescent Unit on Brockway Road, the same road Quintilian School fronts, about 400m away. By comparison, Frankland Centre's own compound — WA's one existing secure forensic facility — covers roughly 1.4–1.6 hectares, around two football pitches. Under two football pitches today; close to five more of new secure, cleared, security-managed ground joining it — over three times the current footprint, on two of Mount Claremont's busier roads.

title: The government's environmental reports: what they settle, and what they don't
body: Three consultant reports behind the EPBC referral are now on the site. On trees and black cockatoos the work looks properly done — 114 trees measured individually, checked against Commonwealth guidelines — and we've said so rather than pretend otherwise. But the same reports show the development area clips the State heritage boundary, flag that a Heritage Impact Statement may be needed, and assume a Development Application is coming — the very thing the government's public fact sheet still describes as only a possibility. They also map the security zones for the first time: three concentric buffer zones around the buildings, including a 10-metre "perimeter sterile zone."

title: Filed: the planning pathway FOI — will there ever be a Development Application?
body: Lodged with the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage. It asks directly whether a Development Application is required for the Graylands Campus Project or the CTRC relocation, whether public consultation applies to any approval step, whether the project has been referred to the Heritage Council under the Heritage Act 2018, and for any document recording anticipated approval milestones. Covers both the main Graylands site and the CTRC relocation site, from January 2021 to date.

title: New: Graylands has done this before — 1991, a picket, and a government promise
body: This isn't the first time this site has changed. In 1980, forensic patients were already on-site. In 1989, government decided to build a dedicated maximum-security unit, and John XXIII parents organised against it. Government responded with a real, dated, advertised consultation process for a single 30-bed addition. What's proposed now is an order of magnitude larger, and it isn't an addition — it replaces the institution. The full history is now on the site, with maps and photographs from the record, and it runs through what this means for site selection, heritage protection, and the scale of consultation this decision actually warrants.

title: New: every government contract for this project, in one place
body: Every contract for planning, design and early works on this project since October 2022 is now compiled from the government's own contract-disclosure register, with a saved copy of each record. One thing stood out enough to add to Concern 6: of every contract on that register, not one is for community, resident or school engagement.

title: OMID's own fact sheet now says what consultation it considers “required” — and residents aren't in it
body: OMID's project fact sheet was reissued in September 2026 with a new question: “What consultation is required?” Its answer names only the clinical and design consultation mandatory under hospital-authorisation standards; public consultation is described as something that may occur incidentally through an unrelated planning process, and community engagement only as something that may happen once construction risks disrupting neighbours. That's now the government's own stated position on what this project owes the community — not an oversight this campaign can ask to be corrected.

title: New: WA's own psychiatrists say Graylands “will not deliver” enough beds
body: The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists' WA Branch says the state's forensic mental health system is genuinely “gridlocked” — and that the redeveloped Graylands campus “will not deliver the number of beds sufficient for future needs.” This campaign agrees WA needs more forensic capacity. The question is whether one 176-bed campus, at this site, is the right way to provide it. Concern 8 has been rewritten around this finding.

title: New: the government has consulted on this exact site before
body: In 1993, before the Frankland Centre opened, the Health Minister publicly promised the community would be consulted on admission guidelines — and followed through with newspaper advertisements, media information, and letters and pamphlet drops. No equivalent process has been identified for a transformation many times larger.

title: Research paper updated: a Cabinet-approved plan we didn't know about
body: A government tender document revealed that an updated business case was approved and Cabinet approved a Project Definition Plan for this project in November 2025 — after the site was chosen, and after the law changed. The research paper has been rewritten around this finding, corrected on how it describes leave and reintegration under the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023, and tightened in several other places. Full detail in the paper.

title: New: a dedicated page for journalists
body: A new Media page sets out this campaign's position in one place for reporters — what we are and aren't asking for, a sourced fact sheet, and a named contact — so coverage doesn't default to a 'residents vs a mental health facility' frame.

title: New: the odour buffer question
body: A new page sets out a statutory planning restriction we haven't discussed before — the City of Nedlands' own scheme says no sensitive land use, hospitals included, is to be located in the Subiaco Wastewater Treatment Plant odour buffer that Infrastructure WA says this site falls within. We've checked the government's own referral documents and correspondence directly, and set out exactly what's confirmed, what's missing, and what we've asked to see.

title: New: The Site — plans, drawings and the published timeline, all in one place
body: A new page collects the actual architectural plans for the expansion, the government's own masterplan diagram, and the published procurement and construction timeline — including the newest Managing Contractor tender documents and what's now visibly under way on the ground. It will grow as more plans and evidence become available.
linkText: See the plans and the timeline

title: Work has started: crews on site at the John XXIII Avenue boundary
body: On 3 September, a resident stopped to speak with a work crew carrying out electrical infrastructure work at the John XXIII Avenue boundary of the Graylands site. Asked what it was for, the crew confirmed it was for the proposed development — the first physical sign of site works that are already commencing. OMID's own current project fact sheet independently confirms the same month for these works, and confirms construction proper still has no set start date.

title: Responding to a letter in the Post
body: A letter published in the Post (29 August) questioned this campaign's position and pointed to the site's long operating history. We've published a full reply on our new Letters & Replies page.

title: First Freedom of Information application filed
body: The first of our eight planned FOI applications — the site selection and due diligence request to the Department of Health — has been lodged (FOI 2026-55). The outcome will be published in full once the statutory 45-day period runs. We've also added a Funding page setting out how this, and future costs, are being paid for.

title: Petition passes 500 signatures
body: The Change.org petition passed 500 signatures on 26 August. Every signature adds weight behind the Legislative Council petition process, and gives Sandra Brewer more to point to when she raises this in Parliament.

title: Safety Risks page added to study the risks posed. Grayland incident log built from evidence.
body: The Safety Risks page looks into how facilities like the proposed Graylands expansion are run and what risks they can pose to the surrounding community. This is based on available data of incidents, comparable facilities and statistics that have been published. Five concerns are stated up front — absconding frequency, transitions between security levels, release and diagnostic error, compliance-dependent leave, and what the CLMI Act's legislated push toward community access actually requires — each linked directly to the log entries and official statistics that support it.

title: Research paper updated: full incident record and official statistics
body: The community research paper has been updated. Section 3 now carries the complete documented incident record for the site, and a new section sets out three official datasets — absconding by facility, assaults on nursing staff by facility, and the offence profile of people held under custody orders — each drawn from Parliamentary answers or statutory annual reports. The executive summary has been rewritten to state the question the paper actually asks: not whether Western Australia needs forensic mental health capacity, but whether anyone has established that this model is safe at this site.

title: Questions on Notice tracker launched
body: Sandra Brewer MLA has followed through on the commitment in her 2 August update: 14 Questions on Notice covering the Project Definition Plan, the Infrastructure WA business case findings, Taskforce meeting dates, campus security, the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 and Department of Justice involvement, bed capacity by type through to 2029, and the relocation of the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre — lodged 11–13 August 2026, all currently awaiting a Ministerial answer. We've built a new page tracking every one, plus the historical questions already on the record, updated as answers land.
linkText: Open the Questions on Notice tracker

title: Letter sent to the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist
body: We wrote to Dr Nathan Gibson, WA’s Chief Psychiatrist — an independent statutory office under the Mental Health Act 2014, distinct from the Ministers and agencies already listed on this site. The letter asks whether the Office was involved in GRAFT or otherwise advised on the decision to retain Graylands as the preferred site, whether site suitability has been formally reviewed since the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 came into force, what school- and community-specific risk, notification and emergency-response arrangements exist, and whether the Chief Psychiatrist would support an independent reassessment of the site. A written response was requested within 14 days.
linkText: Read the letter on the Correspondence page

title: Petition covered in The Post
body: The Post ran a report on the petition in print (15 August 2026, p.14, ‘Petition for Graylands’, Jack Maddern), noting it had reached 368 signatures at the time of writing. The piece reiterated that this is not opposition to forensic mental health services, but a call to pause site works, release the full evidence base, and hold genuine community consultation before construction begins. Asked for comment, Planning Minister John Carey said information had been provided to local stakeholders including a nearby school and the City of Nedlands — the same ‘stakeholders were informed’ framing already noted in his 24 July reply — but again did not say whether a formal round of public consultation would occur.

title: WAtoday covers the campaign: ‘No one was told’
body: WAtoday published a report on the site-selection process and the change in leave conditions under the CLMI Act, with Paul speaking on the record. The government's comment in the piece closely echoes the same language already in Minister Carey's 24 July reply to us — the Taskforce history, the 'more than a decade' of planning — rather than addressing the specific points raised. The City of Nedlands confirmed a letter is going to the Department of Health this week seeking further information.

title: Update received from Sandra Brewer MLA, Member for Cottesloe
body: Ahead of Parliament's return, the local Member sent residents a written update — confirming the current Stage 1 scope, noting the same taskforce also covers the nearby Selby Older Adult Mental Health Service, and setting out a funding history that shows Stage 1 delivery has been pushed back in every State Budget since it was first funded in 2023–24. She's confirmed she'll lodge questions on notice with the relevant Ministers at the August sitting. Full letter now on the Correspondence page.
linkText: Read the full letter on the Correspondence page

title: Door-drop flyer distribution begins
body: Printed flyers are being hand-delivered to households around Mount Claremont, directing residents to the petition and this site. The flyer is now also on the Take Action and Downloads pages, so it can be forwarded electronically to neighbours and shared in local groups. If you'd like flyers for your own street, get in touch.
linkText: Get the flyer from the Downloads page

title: Reply received from Hon John Carey MLA's office
body: Minister Carey's office has replied to our 17 June letter. The reply sets out the project's history and the current Stage 1 scope. We've compared it line by line against our original 17 requests, and checked one of its claims against the source document it names — both are now on the new Correspondence page.

title: Website and petition now live
body: The community website and the Change.org petition have launched. If you're reading this after arriving from the petition, welcome — the concerns behind each ask are set out in full on the Concerns and Sources pages. If you're here first, you can sign the petition from the button at the top of this page.
linkText: Read the concerns behind the petition

title: Reply by Nedlands Council
body: The City of Nedlands has responded to our letter and confirmed that it has had only limited involvement in the Graylands Campus Project to date, has not adopted a formal position on the proposal, and has not been asked to undertake consultation with residents, schools or community groups. The City also indicated that it could take a more proactive role going forward, including seeking further information from the State Government and improving communication with councillors and local stakeholders.

title: Met with Sandra Brewer MLA, Member for Cottesloe
body: Community representatives met with the local Member to raise the governance concerns set out in the Research Paper. She has agreed to consider lodging Questions on Notice to the responsible Ministers on the decision trail, the CLMI Act coordination, and the alternative sites question.
linkText: See what came of this on the Correspondence page

title: Formal letters sent to six State Ministers
body: The community wrote formally to the Ministers for Planning/Housing/Health Infrastructure, Health/Mental Health, Heritage, Environment, Education, and Corrective Services, with a copy to the Premier and Attorney General, setting out the concerns documented in this research and requesting a response within 28 days.
linkText: See who replied on the Correspondence page

title: Letter sent to Sandra Brewer MLA
body: A letter went to the local Member for Cottesloe, requesting she raise these concerns formally in Parliament.
linkText: Follow this thread on the Correspondence page

title: Letter sent to Nedlands Council
body: A letter went to the Nedlands Council Mayor, Councillors and Chief Executive Officer, raising our concerns and requesting for their support to raise these issues to the relevant authorities.
linkText: Follow this thread on the Correspondence page
